## Abstract

Elicitation of HIV broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) by vaccination first requires the activation of diverse precursors, followed by successive boosts that guide these responses to enhanced breadth through the acquisition of somatic mutations. Because HIV bnAbs contain mutations in their B cell receptors (BCRs) that are rarely generated during conventional B cell maturation, HIV vaccine immunogens must robustly engage and expand B cells with BCRs that contain these improbable mutations. Here, we engineered an immunogen that activates diverse precursors of an HIV V3-glycan bnAb and promotes their acquisition of a functionally critical improbable mutation. This immunogen was validated biochemically, structurally, and in three different humanized immunoglobulin mouse models that were designed to test HIV immunogens. These results provide a blueprint for rationally designing priming immunogens that explicitly target the elicitation of antibodies with functional yet improbable mutations.

## Abstract

The goal of HIV vaccine design is to elicit broadly neutralizing antibodies. However, broadly neutralizing antibody responses require that the memory B cells from which they arise acquire several rare somatic mutations. Here, Swanson et al. developed an immunogen with the goal of eliciting these unlikely mutations in antibodies that target the V3-glycan site of the HIV envelope. The authors found that their immunogen, 10.17GS, was able to elicit memory B cell responses enriched for these improbable mutations when given as a vaccine to mice carrying human immunoglobulin receptor genes. These data, further validated with biochemical and structural analysis, demonstrate that we can change the odds of HIV vaccine success. —Courtney Malo

## INTRODUCTION

The induction of broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) remains a main goal of human immunodeficiency (HIV) vaccine development efforts. There are multiple examples of these antibodies, isolated from people living with HIV, which target conserved epitopes on the HIV envelope (Env) surface glycoprotein and offer protection against HIV acquisition. Thus, current vaccine design efforts are focused on eliciting high and durable titers of such protective antibodies (1–6). A promising approach to generate a successful HIV vaccination regimen involves multiple immunizations, starting with a priming step that activates the precursors of target bnAbs, followed by sequential boosting vaccinations to mature such antibodies to breadth (7–10). The robust priming of bnAb lineages is considered a critical step for a successful HIV vaccine, because starting with a large and diverse pool of precursors will increase the chance of maturing at least some of them into bnAbs through additional boosting vaccinations. Recent studies have demonstrated the feasibility of priming bnAb lineages in various models, including knockin (KI) mice (11–13), outbred nonhuman primates (NHPs) (14, 15), or, more recently, humans (16–18). For example, Williams et al. (18) reported the induction of bnAb B cell lineages that targeted the membrane proximal external region (MPER) of gp41 and neutralized 15% of heterologous global HIV strains and 35% of clade B HIV strains. However, maturing these activated precursors into bnAbs remains a challenge.

After priming, activated precursors typically need to acquire a large number of somatic mutations to develop neutralization breadth and potency (19). Some of these acquired mutations are considered improbable, because they are unlikely to occur in vivo given their locations in “cold” spots of the immunoglobulin (Ig) genes that are rarely targeted by activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) or because they require multiple nucleotide changes to introduce the amino acids present in the mature antibody (20). Improbable mutations are enriched in all HIV bnAb lineages (20, 21). Despite recent progress, guiding antibodies to acquire rare mutations by vaccination represents an ongoing challenge for HIV vaccine development. One promising strategy to achieve this goal aims to engineer immunogens that preferentially interact with antibodies containing the desired rare mutations, thus providing a binding and activation advantage for B cells with B cell receptors (BCRs) containing the target improbable mutations.

The V3-glycan epitope on HIV Env is a conserved site engaged by diverse bnAbs such as DH270.6, BG18, and PGT121. These antibodies neutralize between 55 and 65% of HIV isolates and use long heavy-chain complementarity determining region 3 (CDRH3) loops to contact the epitope, which includes the base of the Env V3 loop and two glycans located at positions 332 and 301 (3, 22–25). Precursors of V3-glycan bnAb B cell lineages are rare in the BCR repertoire (11), and, thus, successful priming of V3-glycan bnAbs is a major focus of HIV vaccine design. Priming immunogens have previously been developed that activate precursors of V3-glycan bnAbs in animal models (11, 15, 26–31). Once activated, these precursors need to acquire between 10 and 20 somatic mutations to become bnAbs. For DH270.6 lineage antibodies, our previous work showed that only 12 mutations, of which 10 are improbable, are sufficient to recapitulate the full breadth and potency of the mature bnAb (32). From these mutations, the improbable substitution of glycine with arginine at heavy-chain position 57 (G57RHC) plays an outsized role in breadth development; previous analysis of this lineage suggests that the random probability of an R mutation occurring at this position is ~1% (20, 21). Although such mutations may occur infrequently, strong antigenic selection of such a mutation is likely required for it to be present on a large number of BCRs in the repertoire (15, 32). Structural and functional analyses revealed that R57HC interacts with the conserved GDIR/K motif in the Env V3 loop and is required for the neutralization of Envs with V1 loops of variable lengths by DH270 lineage antibodies, an essential function for breadth (20, 33, 34). Other V3-glycan loop bnAbs, such as BG18 and PGT121, also contain an arginine residue that interacts with the conserved V3 GDIR/K motif like G57RHC in DH270.6. Although these arginines are germline-encoded in the light chains of BG18 and PGT121, their structural similarity to R57HC in DH270.6 suggests an epitope recognition mechanism that is common across V3-glycan bnAbs. For the induction of a polyclonal response against the conserved V3-glycan epitope by vaccination, it may be advantageous to develop immunogens that elicit antibodies containing arginine residues that are functionally homologous to R57HC in DH270.6.

The CH848 10.17DT HIV envelope, hereafter called 10.17DT, is a previously engineered SOSIP immunogen that successfully primes and activates precursors of the DH270.6 bnAb lineage (15). In a mouse KI model expressing the DH270 unmutated common ancestor (DH270 UCA3), 10.17DT activated target B cells and promoted their maturation through the acquisition of key mutations necessary for neutralization breadth and potency (15). The G57RHC substitution was observed in ~1% of the activated precursors from DH270 UCA3 KI mice primed with the 10.17DT SOSIP, implying that there was limited selection for arginine at this position (15). Although this immunogen performs well in animal models, it would be beneficial to further increase its ability to activate precursors in more diverse genetic backgrounds and to promote the acquisition of the G57RHC mutation in a higher proportion of elicited antibodies. In this study, we used structural analysis and computational modeling to redesign the V1 loop of 10.17DT toward this goal. The resulting immunogen was validated biochemically, structurally, and in multiple animal models.

## RESULTS

### Design of a 10.17DT SOSIP variant with a short V1 loop

The previous design of a DH270 priming immunogen was based on a natural HIV envelope called 10.17, which was isolated from an individual who developed the DH270 lineage antibodies during chronic HIV-1 infection (15). This Env was stabilized with the typical SOSIP mutations, and two glycosylation sites from the V1 loop were removed (N133D and N138T) to improve access of DH270 antibodies to the epitope (15). The high-resolution structure of 10.17DT in complex with DH270 UCA3 revealed close packing interactions between the antibody CDRH2 and the V1 loop (Fig. 1A) (34). This is in contrast with the interaction of 10.17DT with the mature DH270.6 antibody, where the V1 loop rearranges away from the interface (Fig. 1B). The mature bnAb can bind to Envs with variable V1 loop lengths, which is essential for its breadth (33). Introducing the G57RHC mutation in DH270 UCA3 causes the rearrangement of the V1 loop and exposes the backbone of V3 loop residue G324 that R57HC contacts (Fig. 1C). The interaction of the 10.17DT V1 loop with DH270 UCA3 is important for high affinity because the natural 10.17 SOSIP, which contains two glycans on the V1 loop that are predicted to clash with the antibody, has a threefold weaker affinity for UCA3 than 10.17DT (1.4 μM versus 455 nM) (15). We hypothesized that the position of the 10.17DT V1 loop in the UCA3 complex limits the ability of this immunogen to interact with antibodies that acquired the G57RHC mutation, because the V1 loop needs to undergo a substantial rearrangement to accommodate arginine at that position. We reasoned that shortening the V1 loop may lead to an improved 10.17DT variant that better exposes the binding site of R57HC and may promote the acquisition of the G57R HC mutation with higher frequency in activated DH270 precursors. RosettaRemodel was used to test different 10.17DT V1 loop truncation points and various linkers to reconnect them in silico (35). Joining the V1 loop at residues A127 and V149 with a “GSGG” linker was predicted to be the most energetically favorable. In the model of this 10.17DT variant, called 10.17GS, the V1 loop did not contact the UCA3 antibody and left exposed the base of the V3 loop where R57HC is expected to bind (Fig. 1, C and D).

### Biophysical characterization of the engineered 10.17GS SOSIP immunogen

10.17GS was expressed recombinantly and purified as a SOSIP Env. Negative-stain electron microscopy analysis showed that 10.17GS forms well-ordered trimers, and binding studies confirmed that it has the same antigenic profile as 10.17DT (fig. S1). Therefore, the V1 loop truncation did not substantially affect the overall stability or epitope presentation of 10.17GS compared to 10.17DT. 10.17GS bound UCA3 with a similar equilibrium dissociation constant as 10.17DT (KD of 420 versus 455 nM), suggesting that the loss of V1 loop contacts in 10.17GS does not affect binding to this inferred precursor (Fig. 2A). 10.17GS also bound the glycan-V3 antibodies BG18 and PGT121 but did not engage their inferred precursors, similar to 10.17DT (fig. S1F). A UCA3 antibody that contained the G57R mutations in the heavy chain (DH270 UCA3 + G57R) had a fivefold higher affinity for 10.17GS than that for 10.17DT (Fig. 2A). The binding improvements were primarily due to a faster on-rate (7860 Ms−1 versus 2477 Ms−1), consistent with the presence of a preformed binding site for R57 in 10.17GS that does not need V1 loop rearrangements as required for complex formation with 10.17DT. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) binding of 10.17GS and 10.17DT to UCA3 and to UCA3, plus combinations of functionally improbable mutations, confirmed that 10.17GS provides an advantage to other antibodies bearing mutations known to play a critical role in DH270.6 neutralization breadth (Fig. 2B and fig. S1G). Binding was also measured against DH270 UCA4, a more probable inference of the DH270.6 unmutated common ancestor computed from a clonal lineage containing six members, whereas only five sequences were available when UCA3 was determined (33). The only sequence difference between DH270 UCA3 and DH270 UCA4 is in the CDRH3 loop, with serine at position 103 being replaced by glycine in UCA4. 10.17GS had 15-fold lower binding affinity for UCA4 than that for UCA3 (KD of 6.8 μM versus 420 nM) (Fig. 2A). Nevertheless, this interaction was twofold higher than that of 10.17DT with UCA4, suggesting improved recognition of more diverse CDRH3 loops by 10.17GS.

Given that the CDRH3 loop is the main mediator of Env recognition for V3-glycan bnAbs, the ability of a candidate immunogen to engage a broad human precursor pool is contingent upon its recognition of BCRs with diverse CDRH3 loops. To evaluate the potential of 10.17DT and 10.17GS to engage DH270.6 precursors with diverse CDRH3 loops, we used a previously described single-site saturation mutagenesis library that contains every single–amino acid substitution in the CDRH3 loop of UCA3 (36). High-throughput screening of this library on the surface of yeast identified the CDRH3 loop mutations that are recognized by 10.17DT. On the basis of these experimental data, ~85 million human BCR sequences were evaluated in silico for their predicted ability to bind the 10.17DT immunogen. Each sequence was aligned to the reference DH270 UCA CDRH3 loop, and the binding effects of each mutation, as determined by library screening, were added together. To assess whether 10.17GS could recognize more diverse CDRH3 loops than 10.17DT, we screened the DH270 UCA3 CDRH3 loop library with these two immunogens in parallel. CDRH3 loop single-site scFv mutants of UCA3 were displayed on the surface of yeast, labeled with 10.17DT or 10.17GS SOSIPs, and isolated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) (Fig. 2, C and D, and fig. S2A). Clones that showed binding above background were sorted, and, after expansion, their DNA was isolated and analyzed by next-generation sequencing. The frequencies of a given substitution in the original library and the sorted clones were compared to determine whether a mutation was beneficial or detrimental to immunogen binding (Fig. 2E and tables S1 and S2).

To validate the results of the library screen, we produced seven point-mutant UCA3 antibodies as recombinant IgGs and compared their binding to 10.17GS and 10.17DT by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) with their enrichment in the library screen (fig. S2, B and C). Although we observed a good overall agreement between the two measurements, one CDRH3 mutation of interest, S103G, the only sequence difference between DH270 UCA3 and UCA4, showed opposite effects in the two assays. This mutation was predicted by library screening to be favorable for 10.17GS binding [log2(enrichment) = 1.0] but unfavorable for 10.17DT [log2(enrichment) = −2.3] (fig. S2D). However, when true 1:1 binding measurements were conducted with recombinant S103G Fab, a reduction in KD was noted for both 10.17DT and 10.17GS (Fig. 2A). This discrepancy was likely due to avidity effects present in the library screening measurements but absent in the SPR analysis. ELISA measurements that capture avidity contributions showed strong binding of S103G IgG to 10.17GS but weak binding to 10.17DT, in agreement with the library display data (fig. S2E). As illustrated here and shown by others, discrepancies between binding measurements by deep mutational libraries and true 1:1 dissociation constants may occur because of the different experimental platforms that use distinct antibody formats [FACS of scFvs (single-chain variable fragments) displayed on the surface of yeast versus SPR of recombinant Fabs] (32, 37, 38).

One hundred seventy-nine total UCA3 CDRH3 loop substitutions maintained or improved baseline 10.17GS binding compared with 115 for 10.17DT (Fig. 2F and tables S1 and S2). The DH270.6 CDRH3 loop is composed of 20 amino acids, of which 6 are templated by the D3–2 2 gene and 9 are encoded by N nucleotides added at random by the terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) enzyme during V(D)J recombination (36). 10.17GS recognized more substitutions than 10.17DT at the nine CDRH3 loop sites encoded by N-nucleotide additions (Fig. 2G). This is important because random nucleotide addition during V(D)J recombination is the largest contributor to CDRH3 loop diversity. For an immunogen to recognize diverse CDRH3 loops, it therefore must engage a wide variety of amino acids in these nontemplated regions.

We next performed bioinformatic analysis to identify the frequency of CDRH3 loops recognized by 10.17DT or 10.17GS from a database of ~85 million human BCRs. Because the number of natural sequences available was limited relative to the size of the human immune repertoire (>1012), we also queried a database of more than 180 billion synthetic IgG sequences generated computationally with IGoR (Inference and Generation of Repertoires) as previously described (36, 39, 40). CDRH3 loop sequences were aligned to UCA3, and mismatches were scored on their predicted ability to bind the target immunogen based on the deep scanning mutagenesis (DSM) substitution profile. Substitutions with log2(enrichment) values above −0.2 were considered favorable for SOSIP binding. Although CDRH3 loops with the same length and D gene reading frame and position as DH270.6 are frequent in the human repertoire (~1:2000), they exhibit diversity in the nontemplated regions encoded by N nucleotides as described above; as such, no sequences that matched the exact CDRH3 loop sequences of DH270 UCA3 were identified. Using the mutagenesis profile, four sequences from the human IgG database were predicted to bind 10.17DT, and 29 were expected to bind 10.17GS, corresponding to projected precursor frequencies of 1:20 million and 1:3 million for 10.17DT and 10.17GS, respectively (fig. S2F). Within the synthetic IGoR dataset, the predicted frequency of engaged precursors was fewer than 1:100 million and 1:33 million for 10.17DT and 10.17GS, respectively (fig. S2F). These results suggested that the newly engineered 10.17GS may engage and activate in vivo a broader pool of precursor antibodies with diverse CDRH3 loops compared with 10.17DT.

### Structural characterization of the engineered 10.17GS SOSIP immunogen

To visualize the interaction of the UCA3 with the V1 loop–engineered 10.17GS SOSIP trimer, we determined a cryo–electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of 10.17GS in complex with DH270 UCA3 at 3.6-Å resolution [Fig. 3A, fig. S3, and table S3; Protein Data Bank (PDB): 9AUH]. The cryo-EM reconstruction obtained without applying any symmetry during the refinement showed three UCA3 molecules bound to the V3-glycan site of the SOSIP Env trimer. UCA3 retained the key contacts with 10.17GS that were observed before in the structure of UCA3 bound to 10.17DT (PDB: 8SAX) (34), including interactions with the N332 glycan. Contacts with the conserved V3 loop 324GDIK327 motif were centered around the UCA3 CDRH1 residue Y33HC that forms hydrogen bonds with D325 and K327 of the SOSIP (Figs. 1A and 3B). The UCA3 CDRH3 tip was nestled into the base of the V3 loop and stacked against glycan N332. The side-chain hydroxyl of CDRH3 residue Y105HC made a hydrogen bond with the side chain of the gp120 residue T415. We had previously reported that the V1 loop in the 10.17DT immunogen sterically hinders the close approach of UCA3 and that its displacement is required to accommodate the G57RHC substitution, allowing the UCA3 + G57RHC antibody to position closer to its epitope (34). For 10.17GS, shortening of the V1 loop removed this steric barrier, allowing UCA3 to bind closer to the paratope even without the G57R mutation, consistent with our design goal. The overall similarity of their paratope contacts supports the comparable measured affinities and interaction mode of UCA3 with 10.17DT and 10.17GS, with the closer approach of UCA3 to its epitope in 10.17GS possibly offsetting the loss of interactions with the V1 loop in 10.17DT.

Incorporation of the critical, improbable G57RHC mutation into UCA3 improved the affinity to 10.17GS by fivefold compared with 10.17DT (Fig. 2A). To understand the structural basis for this higher affinity, we determined a cryo-EM structure of 10.17GS in complex with UCA3 + G57R at 3.8-Å resolution (Fig. 3C, fig. S3, and table S3; PDB: 9AUG). The R57HC residue side chain was well resolved in the cryo-EM reconstruction; it inserted between the V3 and the V1 loops and engaged in hydrogen bonding interaction with G324 of the conserved V3 loop GDIK motif. Although the V3 loop position was similar and well defined in both the 10.17GS-UCA3 and 10.17GS-UCA3 + G57R maps, the shortened V1 loop was disordered in the 10.17GS-UCA3 structure but appeared relatively more ordered in the 10.17GS-UCA3 + G57R structure (fig. S4). A newly formed hydrogen bond between T58 in the CDRH2 loop and S136 in the designed region of the 10.17GS V1 loop was observed that likely stabilized the V1 loop (Fig. 3D). In addition, continuous density between the glycan N156 and the V1 loop was observed in the 10.17GS-UCA3 + G57R, suggesting a role of this glycan interaction in further stabilizing the V1 loop. Together, our results illustrate the structural basis for how the 10.17GS immunogen effectively engages UCA3 and creates an affinity gradient for selecting the critical, improbable G57RHC mutation. The insertion of the R57HC side chain between the V1 and V3 loops resulted in reduced mobility of the flexible V1 loop, further facilitating its interactions with the gp120 glycan N156 and with the antibody through a hydrogen bond with the CDRH2 residue T58HC. This interaction between the designed V1 region and the antibody may have a role in the tighter binding of UCA3 + G57R to the 10.17GS immunogen relative to 10.17DT.

No structure of UCA4 was previously available, because no Env bound it with sufficient affinity. Given that 10.17GS bound tighter to UCA4 than 10.17DT (Fig. 2A), we sought to determine a structure of the UCA4–10.17GS complex to visualize the binding interface of our designed immunogen with this precursor and to understand how V1 loop truncation led to affinity improvements. A structure of this complex was solved at 3.8-Å resolution (Fig. 3E, fig. S3, and table S3; PDB: 9AUI). Comparison of UCA4 and UCA3 in complex with 10.17GS revealed nearly identical binding interfaces (Fig. 3, B and F, and fig. S5A). The CDRH2 loop that harbors the G57HC residue had similar configuration in both UCA3 and UCA4 structures (fig. S5B). The side-chain hydroxyl of residue S103HC in UCA4 makes hydrogen bonds with the main chain carbonyl and nitrogen of residue Y106HC and the main chain nitrogen of Y105HC. Although the configuration of the CDRH3 loop that harbors S103HC (UCA3)/G103HC(UCA4) was similar for the antigen-bound structures of both precursors, interactions mediated by S103HC may stabilize the conformation of the UCA3 CDRH3 loop to facilitate its insertion into the glycan shield at the N332-glycan site, resulting in the faster on-rate (ka) that we observed. The loss of these interactions in UCA4, together with the increased flexibility due to the introduction of a glycine at position 103, may result in a more disordered CDRH3 loop, which may require a higher entropic cost to bind antigen. Residues S103HC (UCA3) and G103 HC (UCA4), the only differing residues between the two precursors, were not directly involved in interaction with Env, suggesting that the shortened V1 loop in 10.17GS is the key facilitator that allows the binding of this Env to UCA4 (Fig. 3G and fig. S5, C and D).

### 10.17GS SOSIP activates DH270 precursors and promotes the acquisition of functional improbable mutations in humanized Ig mice

Previous work described a KI mouse model that expressed the paired, prearranged heavy and light chains of DH270 UCA3 in its BCR repertoire at a frequency of ~30% (15). The 10.17DT and 10.17GS SOSIP immunogens were analyzed in vivo in this model. Immunogens were formulated with 3M052-alum adjuvant in preparation for future NHP studies, given that this adjuvant has been shown to be superior in that model. Groups of six animals were vaccinated four times at 2-week intervals. Blood was collected at the preimmune time point and 1 week after each immunization; spleens were harvested 1 week after the final immunization (Fig. 4A). Splenic B cell phenotyping was conducted after the last immunization to measure the frequency of antigen-specific class-switched IgG B cells in both germinal center (GC)–derived and memory B cells (fig. S6A) using 10.17DT hook sets that had been previously validated (15). The choice to use this probe set, rather than a 10.17GS-specific one, was made to ensure a more stringent analysis of antibodies that can cross-react with 10.17DT and are, therefore, not specific to the V1 loop modifications introduced in 10.17GS. Both 10.17DT and 10.17GS were immunogenic, as evidenced by robust class-switched responses observed in both the memory and GC compartments (Fig. 4B and fig. S6B). Most of these responses targeted the glycan-V3 epitope, as assessed by the loss of binding to 10.17DT knockout (10.17DT KO) (15). This previously described 10.17DT variant lacks the N332 glycan, a key epitope contact of canonical V3-glycan antibodies, including UCA3 and DH260.6 (Fig. 4B and fig. S6, C to E).

Serum ELISAs of the longitudinal samples showed that both 10.17DT and 10.17GS were immunogenic (Fig. 4C and fig. S7A). Epitope-specific responses were calculated by taking the difference between serum binding to 10.17DT and 10.17DT KO (Fig. 4D). Epitope-specific responses were increased by approximately fourfold in 10.17GS-immunized animals compared with 10.17DT-immunized animals after three immunizations (week 5). After the fourth immunization, epitope-specific responses were not different in the 10.17GS and 10.17DT groups, suggesting that fewer shots of 10.17GS were sufficient to induce comparable epitope-specific responses. Detectable titers were elicited by both immunogens against the 10.17 SOSIP trimer (Fig. 4D), the natural Env modified to design 10.17DT, which has fully native and glycosylated V3 and V1 loops. The 10.17 SOSIP is not recognized by DH270 UCA3 or other V3-glycan precursor antibodies, suggesting that precursors activated by 10.17DT or 10.17GS also matured enough to recognize native, glycosylated V1/V3 loops (15, 33). Serum samples from all 10.17DT or 10.17GS animals neutralized 10.17DT pseudovirus, but there was no detectable neutralization of a related pseudovirus that had the N332 glycan deleted, further corroborating that the responses are V3 directed (fig. S7, B and C). Although serum ELISAs showed some recognition of the 10.17 Env, pseudovirus neutralization assays did not detect neutralization breadth beyond the autologous virus. This was expected given that additional mutations beyond G57R are necessary for DH270.6 to acquire breadth (32, 41).

Bulk next-generation sequencing of BCRs from splenic B cells showed that all six 10.17GS-vaccinated animals activated UCA3-like precursors and consistently acquired the key G57R mutation, which was present in an average of 41% of human BCR sequences, with a median value of 46% across the individual animals (Fig. 4E and fig. S7D). Only three of the six animals immunized with 10.17DT had the G57R mutation present in more than 1% of the KI sequences, with an average of 17% and a median value of 1.6%. The consistent acquisition of the G57R mutation in more than 40% of the activated DH270 precursors, on average, upon 10.17GS immunization validates the immunogen design strategy.

Given the improved affinity of 10.17GS for UCA4, we hypothesized that we reached an affinity threshold that would allow the engagement of such BCRs in vivo. To test this, a new KI mouse model was generated, expressing the pre-rearranged UCA4 paired heavy and light chains in ~25% of BCRs (fig. S8, A and B, and table S4). These mice were immunized with 10.17DT or 10.17GS formulated with 3M052-alum (Fig. 4F). Serum ELISAs of longitudinal samples showed that both 10.17DT and 10.17GS were similarly immunogenic and elicited comparable epitope-specific responses (Fig. 4, G and H, and fig. S9). Despite the more than 10-fold reduced affinity of the immunogens for UCA4 compared with UCA3, the magnitude of epitope specific responses was comparable to that of the UCA3 model (Fig. 4, D and H).

Flow cytometry analysis of both the memory and GC B cells after the last immunization showed that there was no difference in the number of 10.17DT antigen-specific B cells between the adjuvant only and 10.17DT-immunized groups in either the GC or memory compartments (Fig. 4I and fig. S10A). In contrast, in the 10.17GS-immunized group, ~25% GC and 13% memory class-switched B cells were 10.17DT antigen specific. In naïve DH270 UCA4 KI mice, we were unable to detect GC B cells labeled with 10.17DT, suggesting that the B cell responses observed here were induced by vaccination (fig. S10B). Therefore, 10.17GS not only activated precursors but also led to their maturation by promoting the acquisition of somatic mutations that facilitated 10.17DT recognition. For four of the six mice immunized with 10.17GS and five of the six mice that received 10.17DT, bulk next-generation sequencing of splenic B cells produced more than 1000 KI sequences, sufficient for mutational analysis. In three 10.17GS-immunized animals, the G57R mutation was found in greater than 85% of human BCR sequences, whereas, in one animal, its occurrence was below 1% (Fig. 4J). In contrast, in four of the five animals immunized with 10.17DT, the frequency of the G57R mutation was below 1%, and only one animal acquired this substitution robustly (17% of sequences) (Fig. 4J and fig. S10C). In addition to G57R, we measured the acquisition of other mutations (G31D, M34I, S55T, and R98T) that were found to be important for the development of breadth in the DH270 lineage and found that 10.17GS elicited them at the same rate as 10.17DT (fig. S10C) (32). Together, these data show that the 10.17GS immunogen can potently activate and drive the maturation of UCA4 precursors in vivo.

### 10.17GS SOSIP activates and expands diverse precursors in a DH270-rearranging mouse model

The improved ability of 10.17GS to engage DH270 precursors with diverse CDRH3 loops in vitro (Fig. 2, E and G) suggested that this immunogen may be able to activate more diverse precursors by vaccination. To test this, we developed a rearranging DH270 mouse model that can generate a range of related precursors for the DH270 lineage. In this model, the hVH1–2 segment and a joined DJH segment of the UCA3 heavy-chain variable region are integrated separately into one mouse IgH allele (fig. S11, A and B, and table S4). Unlike the KI of a pre-rearranged VH, the hVH1–2 and UCA3 DJH segments need to undergo de novo V(D)J rearrangement alongside the endogenous mouse Ig segments, resulting in the diversification of the VH-DJH junction. About 13% hVH1–2 –DH270 UCA3 DJH rearrangements contain 20–amino acid CDRH3s, which correspond in length to that of DH270 UCA3 (fig. S11, C and D). The frequency of UCA3 among total splenic B cells depends on the proportion of IgMa B cells (7%), hVH1–2 usage among IgMa B cells (96%), 20–amino acid CDRH3 of hVH1–2–UCA3 DJH (13%), and UCA3 among 20–amino acid CDRH3 (1 in 252). Multiplication of these parameters yields an expected UCA3 frequency of 1 in 28,846 total splenic B cells (fig. S11E). Previous analysis of the DH270 UCA3 KI pre-rearranged mouse model found that ~30% of splenic B cells were UCA3 (15); thus, in these mice, DH270-like BCRs were ~9000-fold less frequent, presenting a more realistic model for activating DH270-like precursors in an outbred population.

To test whether 10.17GS can prime UCA3-related precursors with diverse CDRH3 loops, we immunized two groups of DH270-rearranging mice four times at 2-week intervals with the 10.17GS SOSIP formulated with GLA-SE (glucopyranosyl lipid adjuvant–stable emulsion) adjuvant or adjuvant alone as a control. GLA-SE was selected for this study because it is a potent agonist of Toll-like receptor 4, which is present on mouse and human B cells, but not NHPs, and thus may be a stronger adjuvant that may aid in B cell activation in the more stringent rearranging mouse model. Blood was collected at the preimmune time point and 1 week after each immunization; bulk splenic B cell sequencing was conducted 1 week after the final immunization (Fig. 5A). Serum ELISAs of the longitudinal samples showed that 10.17GS was immunogenic (Fig. 5B and fig. S12A). All mice immunized with 10.17GS were able to mount an epitope-specific response that was detectable after two immunizations (at week 3) and continued to increase (Fig. 5C). Serum showed neutralization of a 10.17DT but not of a 10.17DT KO pseudovirus, further confirming epitope specificity (fig. S12B). Phenotyping of the GC and memory B cell compartments was conducted after the last immunization, and 10.17GS-specific class-switched B cells were detected in all of the immunized animals (Fig. 5D and fig. S13, A and B). There was approximately the same frequency of antigen-specific GC B cells in this model as there was in the UCA3 KI mice (~4%), although memory responses were approximately six times lower (Figs. 4D and 5D). Together with the ELISA and neutralization results, this shows that 10.17GS is immunogenic in this UCA3-rearranging mouse model and induced detectable V3-glycan epitope responses in all immunized animals.

Bulk next-generation sequencing of splenic B cells was conducted after the final immunization to determine the CDRH3 loop composition of activated precursors and the acquisition of the G57RHC mutation. DH270-like BCRs, defined as containing only human V, D, and J segments, with a CDR3H3 loop of 20 amino acids and containing the exact D gene in the same position as in DH270.6, were analyzed for the presence of the G57RHC mutation. In three animals immunized with adjuvant alone, the median frequencies of G57R acquisition were less than 0.01%; in contrast, the four 10.17GS animals showed robust acquisition of the mutation with a median frequency of 26% among DH270-like antibody sequences as well as the selection of one other key mutation for breadth, G31D (Fig. 5E and fig. S13C). Substantial diversity was observed in the N1 nucleotide region of elicited CDRH3 loops at positions 99 and 100, where full–amino acid diversity is present in the repertoire of these animals, confirming that 10.17GS can activate diverse precursors by vaccination (Fig. 5F). The most observed CDRH3 amino acids at positions 99 and 100 of vaccinated animals were also identified as favorable for 10.17GS binding by DSM. Overall, the seven most common amino acids present in the N1 region of 10.17GS-elicited BCRs, which together make up ~80% of the observed DH270-like sequences, were also identified as favorable for 10.17GS binding by DSM. This suggests that the in vitro binding analysis used in this study was a good predictor of the sequence diversity in the antibodies elicited by vaccination (Figs. 2G and 5F). These results demonstrate that 10.17GS can activate, expand, and drive BCRs to acquire improbable mutations in an animal model with a diverse immune repertoire.

## DISCUSSION

A successful HIV vaccine will require activating bnAb precursors followed by their maturation to breadth through the acquisition of somatic mutations. Although HIV bnAbs acquire a large number of mutations during their development, multiple studies have shown that only a subset of them is typically required for broad and potent neutralization (11, 32, 42). This is the case for two bnAbs that target the conserved V3-glycan epitope on Env, BG18 and DH270.6 (11, 32). For DH270.6, we previously showed that only 12 acquired mutations are sufficient to recapitulate the breadth and function of the mature bnAb, suggesting a more direct path to induce such antibodies by vaccination from activated precursors (36). Nevertheless, most of these functionally critical mutations are improbable, meaning that they arise naturally with low frequency in the GC (20, 36). Therefore, the elicitation of high titers of antibodies containing these rare mutations will likely require the development of immunogens that specifically target antibodies with these rarely occurring substitutions.

Arginine at position 57 in the heavy chain of DH270.6 is an improbable mutation that is essential for breadth (20, 33). This mutation was acquired early during the natural development of the bnAb, and its presence leads to heterologous breadth by allowing the bnAb to engage diverse Env V1 loops and access the conserved V3-glycan loop epitope (33, 34). Here, we developed an immunogen optimized to promote the acquisition of the critical R57HC mutation in activated DH270 precursors. Starting from the previously described DH270.6 germline targeting immunogen 10.17DT, we engineered 10.17GS, which has a shorter V1, using structure-based design and computational modeling (15). In this immunogen, a high-resolution cryo-EM structure confirmed that the interaction site of R57HC is exposed, thus providing a binding energy advantage to elicited antibodies containing this mutation, leading to their selection and expansion. Affinity measurements revealed that 10.17GS binds to DH270 UCA3 containing the R57HC mutation with 14-fold higher affinity than to DH270 UCA3, thus providing an affinity gradient to drive the accumulation of this mutation in activated precursors. Compared with 10.17DT, we demonstrated that, in DH270 UCA3 or UCA4 KI mice immunized with 10.17GS, the activated DH270 precursors have an 8- to 800-fold higher rate of R57 acquisition, with the mutation present in 46 to 87% of DH270 UCA-like sequences. A statistically significant difference between the two groups in the UCA3 mouse model was precluded by the presence in the 10.17DT group of an animal that acquired G57R at a 10-fold higher rate (88%) than any other animals in the same group and at least eightfold higher frequency observed in any animals from two previous studies that tested 10.17DT immunogens in the same mouse model (15). Previous work has shown that the acquisition of 12 mutations is necessary for DH270.6 precursors to develop the full breadth and potency of the mature bnAb, with three others beyond G57R being essential (R98THC, S27YLC, and L48YLC) (32). Additional boosting immunizations will, therefore, be required to mature activated precursors containing R57 elicited by 10.17GS, with candidate immunogens to accomplish this recently described (32, 34, 41).

Beyond the acquisition of improbable mutations, the engagement of precursors with diverse CDRH3 loops represents another block for the elicitation of V3-glycan loop bnAbs. In humans, these immunogens are expected to engage B cells with low frequency, estimated at less than 1 in every 10 million B cells (11, 36). This is likely due to the large sequence diversity in the CDRH3 loop of the target BCRs that these immunogens must engage. In contrast, priming immunogens that target other classes of HIV bnAbs whose antigen recognition modes are not CDRH3 dominated, such as VRC01, a CD4 binding site bnAb, engage human B cells at an estimated frequency of 1 in 300,000 and showed robust precursor activation in a phase I clinical trial (16, 17, 43). Given the markedly smaller precursor pool that V3-glycan bnAb priming immunogens can engage, additional optimization will likely be necessary for consistent and robust activation of target BCRs in humans. DSM revealed that 10.17GS recognizes more diverse CDRH3 loops in vitro compared with 10.17DT, leading to a predicted precursor engagement frequency of 1:3 million B cells for this new immunogen, according to our bioinformatic analysis. To test the ability of 10.17DT to engage DH270.6 precursors with diverse CDRH3 loops, we developed a new DH270 mouse model that allows the rearrangement of the V and DJ segments of the heavy chain. In this model, DH270 precursors contain diverse CDRH3 loops with variable amino acids encoded by the N1 nucleotide region. 10.17GS immunizations led to the recovery of DH270-like BCR sequences with different CDRH3 loops, suggesting that this molecule can also engage and activate diverse precursors in vivo. The dominant CDRH3 loop amino acids observed at the variable positions in the immunized animals matched well with the ones selected in vitro by 10.17GS from the single-site saturation mutagenesis libraries. Therefore, high-throughput screening of antibody libraries with a target immunogen can be useful to predict acquired antibody mutations in vivo and may be used as an initial validation step to ensure that vaccine candidates favor the selection of antibodies with target mutations.

To induce DH270.6-like bnAbs, 10.17GS could be used to prime DH270.6 precursors and start their maturation by promoting the acquisition of the R57 mutation, followed by “boosting” with previously described immunogens (32, 41). Compared with other glycan-V3 bnAbs like BG18 or PGT121, DH270.6 does not undergo insertions and deletion during its maturation and requires fewer acquired mutations for breadth, which may facilitate its induction by vaccination. However, unlike bnAbs targeting the CD4 binding site or MPER, glycan-V3 monoclonals have more limited breadth. Therefore, a protective vaccine targeting this epitope will likely need to induce multiple bnAb lineages as part of a polyclonal response. Because BG18 and PGT121 also contain arginine residues that interact with the same Env residues as R57 in DH270.6, it may be advantageous to use immunogens that favor the elicitation of a polyclonal response against the conserved V3-glycan that contain this molecular feature.

Current V3-glycan priming immunogens use the V1 loop to engage target precursors (11, 44). This may be limiting because mature bnAbs must recognize V1 loops with highly diverse sequences and length to achieve breadth. Therefore, activated precursors specific for the V1 loops of the priming immunogens need to become tolerant of diverse V1 loops during maturation, which may prove challenging. Further, V1 loops are highly immunogenic and typically elicit strain-specific antibodies (11, 45). 10.17GS may address some of these issues because its short V1 loops do not contact DH270.6 precursors. The strategy of shortening the V1 loop could also be transferred to other immunogens to ensure optimal exposure of the V3 loop residues engaged by R57HC. Whether this design strategy can be applied to activate precursors of other glycan-V3 lineages will be determined in future studies but could prove challenging for bnAbs like BG18, where the current germline-targeting immunogen binds through strong V1 loop–mediated contacts. Nevertheless, our work illustrates how controlling the molecular details of antibody-antigen interactions using structure-based design and computational modeling can lead to the elicitation of antibodies with desired characteristics by vaccination, especially as it relates to precursor activation and the acquisition of improbable mutations, two key components of a potential HIV vaccine.

Despite the success of 10.17GS, some limitations of the studies described here need to be addressed before advancing this immunogen to clinical trials. The DH270 UCA3 and UCA4 KI mouse models have frequencies of DH270.6 precursors that are at least two orders of magnitude higher than those present in the naïve human repertoire. The successful testing of 10.17GS in the rearranging mouse model alleviates some of these concerns because DH270 precursors are more diverse in this animal model and closer in abundance to humans. Nevertheless, the DH270 precursor repertoire in these rearranging mice lacks sequence diversity in the N2 nucleotide region connecting the D and J genes. In future studies, the frequency of DH270.6 precursors engaged by 10.17GS will be determined experimentally by FACS of human B cells. Furthermore, 10.17GS immunizations will need to be conducted in outbred NHPs, a model that better approximates the true diversity of the human B cell repertoire.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Study design

The main objective of this study was to engineer an improved HIV V3-glycan bnAb priming immunogen that bound, activated, and expanded a diverse pool of DH270.6 bnAb precursors and promoted their affinity maturation by acquiring key functional mutations. To that end, increased binding affinity to diverse precursors in vitro together with their activation and acquisition of key mutations in vivo was the primary end point of this study. Studies were conducted in in-bred mice that were genetically modified to contain DH270.6 precursors in their immune repertoire. The number of mice in each group was limited by mouse availability and analysis costs. Experiments were conducted with group sizes ranging from three to six female mice that were randomly assigned to groups, blinding was not used, and no experimental replicates were included for animal studies. All data were included in analysis.

### Statistical analyses

Individual-level data are presented in data file S1. Nonparametric statistical tests were used for all pairwise group comparisons to avoid distributional assumptions. Differences between mouse groups were tested for statistical significance using two-sided Wilcoxon Mann-Whitney exact tests at a significance level of 0.05. P values are reported without multiple test corrections, except in the case of the data presented in Fig. 4 (I and J), where a false discovery rate was applied to adjust for multiple test corrections. The Wilcoxon Mann-Whitney exact test was used given the small sample size, which did not enable us to assume a normal distribution. P values are shown as follows: not significant (n.s.) difference, P > 0.05; *P < 0.05; **P < 0.01; and ***P < 0.001.
