# Contribution of Meals and Snacks Provided through the Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP) on Young Children’s Total Dietary Intake

**Authors:** Kelsey L. Kinderknecht; Meghan Zimmer; Rebecca Mozaffarian; Erica L. Kenney

**Affiliations:** Department of Nutrition at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts. | Departments of Nutrition and Social and Behavioral Sciences at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts.

## Abstract

Several federal food assistance programs support children’s nutrition. However, evidence is limited on how the Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP), specifically, contributes to children’s dietary intake.

The study objective was to understand how CACFP meals and snacks contribute to young children’s overall dietary intake on a given day.

A within-person, observational study design was used.

Participants were one- to six-year-old children (n=1004) attending CACFP-participating early care and education (ECE) programs participating in the 2017 U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Study of Nutrition and Activity in Childcare Settings (SNACS).

Daily energy-adjusted food group/specific nutrient intakes were the primary outcome measures, standardized by kilocalories consumed.

Paired t-tests evaluated how a child’s energy-adjusted dietary intake at a CACFP-participating ECE program compared to elsewhere on the same day, and analyses were stratified by duration of attendance at an ECE program and household food security status.

Children attending an ECE program for a full day consumed most of their fruit (54%, SE: 0.02), whole grains (67%, SE: 0.03), and dairy (61%, SE: 0.02) from CACFP meals and snacks. When children ate at full day ECE programs, they consumed significantly more energy-adjusted dairy (0.3 c-eq/1000kcals, 95% CI: 0.12, 0.40) and whole grains (0.1 oz-eq/1000kcals, 95% CI: 0.03, 0.25), and less vegetables (−0.1 c-eq/1000kcals, 95% CI: −0.21, −0.08), protein foods (−0.4 oz-eq/1000kcals, 95% CI: −0.60, −0.26), sodium (−211 mg/1000kcals, 95% CI: −283.1, −139.8), saturated fat (−2.1 g/1000kcals, 95% CI: −2.91, −1.28), and added sugars (−6.8 g/1000kcals, 95% CI: −10.15, −3.54) than when they were not at an ECE program. Patterns in energy-adjusted intake differences remained for those experiencing food security compared to food insecurity except for whole grains; children experiencing food security had a significantly higher consumption of whole grains at a full-day ECE program compared to elsewhere (0.2 oz-eq/1000 kcals, 95% CI: 0.05, 0.26) whereas there was no difference for children experiencing food insecurity.

CACFP meals and snacks support nutritious diets for young children by contributing to higher energy-adjusted intakes of dairy and whole grains, and lower energy-adjusted intakes of sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars compared to what children consume elsewhere. Future research should examine how CACFP can further support nutritious diets for children.

## INTRODUCTION

Developing healthful eating habits during early childhood is important for the prevention of diet-related chronic diseases and overall child health and well-being.1–4 While the nutritional quality of children’s eating patterns has improved over the past several decades, most children still have dietary intakes that do not align closely with the recommended diet for optimal health, such as inadequate intake of whole grains, fruits, and vegetables, and excess intake of added sugars.5–9 Policies that help promote nutritious dietary intake in early care and education (ECE) programs are particularly important for supporting improved dietary intake for young children,10,11 as children consume meals and snacks while in attendance, and 59% of U.S. 3–5 year olds attend ECE programs.12 The Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP) is one such program informed by policy; it is a federal nutrition assistance program in the U.S. that sets nutrition standards and provides financial reimbursements to ECE programs for meals and snacks that meet meal pattern standards established by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA). CACFP served over 4.4 million children in 2024, about 80% of whom were from low-income households,13–15 which are more likely to experience food insecurity, defined as uncertain of having or unable to acquire enough food to meet the needs of all members of their household due to insufficient money or other resources for food over the past year, and have lower diet quality.16–18

However, evidence for CACFP’s impact on children’s diet quality is surprisingly sparse.19 Prior studies have had to rely on small sample sizes, lacked comparison groups, or used unreliable measures of dietary intake.20–23 Moreover, nearly all studies have been limited to assessing dietary intake at ECE only, precluding observation of whether CACFP participation changes children’s overall dietary quality. One recent study started to address this evidence gap, using a nationally representative sample of children attending CACFP programs and validated dietary assessments, finding that children’s intakes aligned more closely with the Dietary Guidelines for Americans on child care days compared to non-child care days,24 but given that non-child care days were weekend days, it is unclear whether this was due to CACFP meals and snacks being more healthful or due to intake on weekends being generally less healthful. To build on prior literature, this study aimed to first estimate how much CACFP meals/snacks contribute to overall intake of key food and nutrient groups in a given day for children attending CACFP-participating ECE programs. This study then estimated whether CACFP meals/snacks contribute relatively more to dietary quality than meals/snacks consumed outside of ECE by comparing children’s intake of key food and nutrient groups from CACFP meals and snacks with their intake during the rest of a given day, using a within-child analytic approach to minimize confounding.

## METHODS

### Data Source and Sample

Data were used from a nationally representative cross-sectional study of children attending CACFP-participating ECE programs in program year 2016–2017 from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Food and Nutrition Services (FNS) sponsored Study of Nutrition and Activity in Child Care Settings (SNACS).25 SNACS study staff collected data on 1,576 children aged 1–6 years old attending a CACFP-participating ECE program with complete dietary intake data on days attending an ECE program and parental informed consent. For this analysis, children with missing parent surveys (n=524), from which necessary sociodemographic variables were measured, were excluded, as well as those where duration at childcare was not reported (n=6) (Figure 1). Children with missing data on household food security status, a key covariate in the analysis, were also excluded (n=42). The data were de-identified and no individuals on the study team had links to identifiers. The research was considered non-human subjects research according to the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health Institutional Review Board (IRB23–0577).

### Measures

#### Primary Outcome.

The primary outcome for this study was children’s dietary intake of complementary foods (not including infant formula and/or breastmilk), characterized by total daily food group/nutrient intakes associated with a health-promoting eating pattern that aligns with the 2015–2020 Dietary Guidelines for Americans, including fruits, vegetables, whole grains, dairy, and protein foods, and limited intakes of saturated fat, sodium, and added sugars.1,3,4 To measure 24-hour dietary intake, a trained ECE provider used a validated meal observation method provided by the SNACS study team to assess children’s dietary intake for food consumed and sourced from the ECE program;26 then, a parent/guardian used a food diary to measure children’s dietary intake for food consumed or sourced from outside the ECE program on the same day. Study staff entered dietary data into SurveyNet (version 4.2), a computerized nutrient analysis software program developed by the USDA Food Surveys Research Group,27 and then linked to the Food and Nutrient Database for Dietary Studies (FNDDS, version 2013–2014).28 Staff used the USDA Food Patterns Equivalents Database (FPED, version 2013–2014) to calculate the food pattern equivalents, the quantity of a food component consumed using standardized units (e.g. oz-eq, c-eq) for all foods/ingredients.29 For children with 2 days of dietary intake data on a day attending an ECE program (n=86), the outcome measures were averaged across the 2 days.

#### Sociodemographic characteristics.

Parents provided information on child’s duration of attendance at an ECE program [defined as full day (>5 hours/day) or part day (1–5 hours/day)], age (1–6 years old), sex (male or female), race/ethnicity [non-Hispanic white, non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, or other (including Asian, American Indian/Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander)], household income, household size, number of children in the household, receipt of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in the past 30 days (yes/no), and receipt of Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) in the past 30 days (yes/no).30,31 The parent survey collected data on risk of household food insecurity using the 2-item Hunger Vital Sign screener.32 Household food security status was dichotomized as food secure or food insecure, with risk of food insecurity operationalized as affirmative responses (‘often true’ or ‘sometimes true’) to either or both of the following statements: “within the past 12 months we worried whether our food would run out before we got money to buy more” and “within the past 12 months the food we bought just didn’t last and we didn’t have money to get more.”32 Variables from a survey completed by the sample children’s ECE providers supplied information on whether the child attended a metropolitan area location (yes/no), type of geographic area of program where child attended (rural, small town, suburban, and urban), and whether the child attended a Head Start program (yes/no).33

### Statistical Analysis

To characterize the overall influence of CACFP on children’s total dietary intake in a given day, the proportion of children’s food group intake (fruits, vegetables, whole grains, dairy, and protein foods) in ounce or cup equivalents, and select nutrient intakes [sodium (milligrams), saturated fat (grams), and added sugars (grams)] were calculated by location (ECE program versus elsewhere). In sensitivity analyses, we assessed for differences in dietary outcomes between children with and without parent survey data. To test whether intake from CACFP meals/snacks was of higher nutritional quality than intake outside of the ECE program, we first calculated energy-adjusted dietary intake of the same selected food and nutrient groups above, stratified by ECE and non-ECE intakes, by dividing intake of each group by kcals consumed over the entire day (ECE and non-ECE combined). We then compared these energy-adjusted intakes of key foods and nutrients between meals/snacks consumed at ECE compared to non-ECE intake on the same day using paired t-tests. We stratified by full- or part-day attendance to account for the different amount of exposure to CACFP meals and snacks (full day: >5 hours; part day: 1–5 hours). Differences by household food security status were tested in secondary analyses to examine how consumption of meals and snacks at and away from the ECE program differed for children experiencing risk of food insecurity. Two-sided alpha was set at p <0.05.

All analyses were conducted in R version 4.4.0.34 Child-level sampling weights were used to account for the multi-stage stratified sampling strategy, clustered sampling design, and non-response bias of ECE program providers and children within classrooms.25

## RESULTS

The analytic sample included 1004 children 1–6 years old who attended 242 CACFP-participating ECE programs, had complete parent surveys and dietary intake data on days the child attended an ECE program, and had complete information on risk of household food security status (Table 1). This amounted to 64% of the original full sample (Figure 1). Most study participants were from households with incomes ≤185% of the federal poverty level (59% for full day attendance, 77% for part day attendance) and not experiencing household food insecurity (83% for full day attendance, 55% for part day attendance), with a greater proportion of children who attended a part day program being food insecure, income ≤185% of the federal poverty level, and attending a Head Start center. On average, children attending full day programs consumed 1462 kcals (SE: 52) over an entire day and 603 kcals (SE: 23) while at ECE (43% of daily energy; SE: 0.01), and children attending part day programs consumed 1540 kcals (SE: 25) over an entire day and 422 kcals (SE: 35) while at ECE (28% of daily energy; SE 0.02) (Table 1 and Figure 2).

While most children consumed at least some vegetables, fruits, dairy, whole grains, and protein foods during the entire day, a few children did not (Figure 2). Among children attending a full day ECE program who consumed a nonzero amount, children, on average, consumed 54% of their total fruit intake (SE: 0.02), 67% of their total whole grain intake (SE: 0.03), 61% of their total dairy intake (SE: 0.02), 44% of their total vegetable intake (SE: 0.02), and 41% of their total protein food intake (SE: 0.03) from CACFP meals or snacks served at the ECE program (Figure 2). For dietary components to consume in moderation, on average over an entire day, children consumed 44% of their total added sugar intake (SE: 0.04), 42% of their total saturated fat intake (SE: 0.02), and 44% of their total sodium intake (SE: 0.01) from CACFP meals and snacks served at the ECE program. For part-day attendees, on average over the entire day, children consumed slightly lower proportions of total daily intake of food components and nutrients from CACFP meals and snacks (Figure 2). Supplemental Table 2 shows differences in proportions of intake between children with and without completed parent survey data.

Children attending a full day ECE program, on average, consumed significantly more energy-adjusted dairy (0.3 c-eq/1000 kcals, 95% CI: 0.12, 0.40) and whole grains (0.1 oz-eq/1000 kcals, 95% CI: 0.03, 0.25) and less vegetables (−0.1 c-eq/1000 kcals, 95% CI: −0.21, −0.08), protein foods (−0.4 oz-eq/1000 kcals, 95% CI: −0.60, −0.26), sodium (−211 mg/1000 kcals, 95% CI: −283.1, −139.8), saturated fat (−2.1 g/1000 kcals, 95% CI: −2.91, −1.28), and added sugars (−6.8 g/1000 kcals, 95% CI: −10.15, −3.54) from CACFP meals and snacks compared to intake from all other meals and snacks consumed that day outside of the child care program (Table 3). Meanwhile, children attending a part day ECE program, on average, consumed significantly less energy-adjusted fruits, vegetables, dairy, protein, sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars from CACFP meals and snacks compared to intake from all other meals and snacks consumed that day outside of the child care program (Table 3).

In stratified analyses, all patterns of energy-adjusted differences in intake remained for children attending a full day ECE program experiencing household food security compared to food insecurity, with the exception of intake of whole grains. Children experiencing food security had a significantly higher consumption of whole grains at an ECE program compared to elsewhere (0.2 oz-eq/1000 kcals, 95% CI: 0.05, 0.26) whereas there was no difference in whole grain intake at ECE compared to elsewhere for children experiencing food insecurity (Table 4). For children attending a part day program by food security status, all patterns in energy-adjusted differences remained except for dairy. Children experiencing food security had a significantly lower consumption of dairy at an ECE program compared to elsewhere (−0.3 c-eq/1000kcals, 95% CI: −0.55, −0.05) whereas there was no difference in dairy intake at an ECE program compared to elsewhere for children experiencing food insecurity (Table 5).

## DISCUSSION

This study found that meals and snacks served at CACFP-participating ECE programs support nutritious dietary intakes for young children by contributing a greater amount of energy-adjusted whole grains and dairy intake for children attending full day ECE programs and a lesser amount of sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars for children attending both full day and part day ECE programs. At the same time, however, energy-adjusted intake of vegetables was lower from CACFP meals and snacks for full day attendees, and energy-adjusted intake of fruit and vegetables was lower for part-day attendees. Lower consumption of sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars at ECE programs is particularly important, as lower intakes of these nutrients have been associated with improved cardiometabolic health.35–37 Patterns of energy-adjusted differences remained when comparing children experiencing food security to those experiencing food insecurity; however, children from households experiencing food security consumed a significantly greater amount of whole grains while at a full day ECE program compared to elsewhere, whereas there was no difference in whole grain consumption observed for children experiencing household food insecurity.

This study’s results build on prior research on the link between receiving CACFP meals and snacks and children’s dietary intake.21,22,24 A recent systematic review of studies comparing dietary intake between CACFP-participating and nonparticipating ECE programs showed limited and mixed evidence on the association of CACFP meals and snacks on children’s dietary intake, but indicated that at least some studies found CACFP participation was associated with no differences in fruit consumption, slight increases in vegetable consumption, slight increases in whole grain consumption, lower consumption of protein foods, and increases in milk consumption.19 Similarly, this study found no differences in fruit consumption, greater whole grain consumption, greater dairy consumption, and lower consumption of protein foods from CACFP meals and snacks compared to elsewhere; however, this study found slightly lower vegetable consumption for children attending full day ECE programs. On balance, however, the results suggest that CACFP meals and snacks tend to be more healthful than what is consumed outside of CACFP-participating ECE programs, particularly with regard to lower sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars. While CACFP standards at the time did not explicitly limit sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars, the program’s emphasis on serving dairy, fruits, and vegetables, and overall emphasis on supporting children’s nutrition, may have resulted in ECE programs serving fewer foods high in these nutrients relative to what children are fed in the absence of CACFP standards. Even greater energy-adjusted differences were observed for these nutrients for children attending part day programs (i.e. higher intakes of foods that should be limited consumed away from childcare than at childcare) compared to full day programs, suggesting that, if children attending part day programs had more exposure to CACFP meals and snacks in full day programs, this may be associated with lower intakes of nutrients that should be limited over the entire day.

At the same time, our results suggest CACFP could be further strengthened. Energy-adjusted vegetable intake from CACFP meals and snacks for children attending full day ECE programs was not meaningfully different than what was consumed outside of ECE programs – and all of it was low, likely due to the bitter or undesirable taste of some vegetables and less exposure and familiarity with vegetables among children.38 Meanwhile, a substantial number of children in this study never ate a whole grain throughout the course of their entire day. While CACFP’s meal pattern standards were updated in 2017,39 it is possible that these standards are not yet strong enough to meaningfully improve young children’s diets – a possibility which has been borne out by mixed evidence from several studies that have directly evaluated the standards changes.40,41 It is also possible, however, that ECE providers simply need more support for serving health-promoting, appealing foods, given they face extraordinary barriers for ECE programs to implement CACFP.42 Research should continue to explore how best to support ECE providers so that, in turn, they are best able to provide necessary nutritious and tasty foods to the children they serve.

Strengths of the study include the use of data from SNACS, a nationally representative dataset of children attending CACFP-participating ECE programs. Another strength was the use of reliable and valid methods to measure children’s dietary intake across a 24 hour period, particularly the use of meal observations while at ECE.26 Other studies attempting to measure young children’s dietary intake over a 24 hour period often only use parental-reported 24 hour recalls, which can be difficult when parents do not know what their child actually ate while at an ECE program. Using within-child analyses eliminated potential confounding from children’s individual characteristics that might influence dietary intake (e.g. age, sex, race/ethnicity) that would be inherent in a between-child analysis (i.e. where children who consume CACFP meals and snacks are compared in aggregate with children who do not). This approach also allows us to avoid comparing ECE program days to weekend days, when children’s intakes may be substantially different regardless of ECE participation, and thus allow us to better isolate CACFP’s potential impact on a given child’s diet given the available data. Limitations include missingness on the parent survey for about one third of the initial study sample that had complete dietary outcome data. When comparing dietary outcome data between groups with missing and non-missing parent survey data, there were differences between daily proportions of whole grain and dairy consumption from CACFP meals and snacks. If these differences were not due to lack of stratification on length of CACFP attendance (since this variable was not available for children without parent survey data), these differences may have contributed to a conservative estimate of the average difference in whole grain consumption and an overestimate of the average difference in dairy consumption between what is consumed at ECE program compared to elsewhere. While parent-reported food diaries have been shown to be a reliable and valid measure to collect young children’s dietary intake, there is still potential for misclassification, specifically underreport of foods/beverages consumed, although this is likely to not be differential across children.43 The majority of children only had one day of dietary intake, which could lead to measurement error. Using two different dietary data collection methods to compare dietary intakes at ECE programs (meal observation) compared to elsewhere (parent-reported food diary) could lead to misclassification; however, the misclassification would be consistent for all children. While it is a limitation that breastmilk intake was likely not captured and it is possibly part of some children’s diets in the study sample, prior research has shown that breastfeeding and infant formula consumption tapers into being such a small contribution to children’s overall diets for children 12 months and older that it would only minimally influence the estimates.44 Another limitation is the age of the SNACS-I data; at the time of analysis, results from SNACS-II had not yet been released and to our knowledge the data were not yet publicly available (initial findings were released in July 2025), so the best dataset available for the research question was SNACS-I. While CACFP’s nutrition standards were modified after these data were collected, potentially making the data outdated, research that has examined pre/post changes in CACFP menu offerings and intake have largely found only minimal changes as a result of the standards.40,41 However, future research should evaluate whether CACFP’s contributions to children’s daily intakes have changed using more updated data as it becomes available. Future research should also incorporate consistent dietary assessment methods for children with longitudinal designs, repeated measures, and comparing children attending CACFP-participating and non-participating ECE programs.

## CONCLUSION

Meals and snacks served at CACFP-participating ECE programs significantly contribute to nutritious diets for young children. To isolate the impact of CACFP on young children’s dietary intake, future research should compare dietary intake at and away from an ECE program for children who attend CACFP-participating compared to non-CACFP participating programs. Future research should also examine strategies to expand access to CACFP for ECE providers, further improve the program to support nutritious diets, and ultimately improve reach of CACFP to young children who could benefit from the meals and snacks.

# Statewide Universal School Meals Policies and Food Insecurity: Difference-in-Differences Analysis

**Authors:** Kelsey L. Kinderknecht; Eric B. Rimm; S. Bryn Austin; Shoba Ramanadhan; Matthew M. Lee; Erica L. Kenney

## Abstract

The National School Lunch and Breakfast Program, a US program that addresses food insecurity, requires children with higher household incomes to pay for meals. It is unclear whether universal school meals (USM) policies, which make all meals free, further alleviate food insecurity, particularly for students who would otherwise pay. This study estimates the association between statewide USM policies and food insecurity.

A difference-in-differences study using a nationally representative sample of US households with 6- to 17-year-old children from 2012 to 2021 and 2023 to 2024. The exposure was maintaining statewide USM policy after 2022, determined based on state of residence. The primary outcome was household food insecurity; the secondary outcome was child food insecurity. Analyses were stratified by household income.

The sample included 75 122 households. Households with the highest incomes in USM-maintaining states experienced a 1.3-percentage-point (95% CI: −2.1, −0.5) differential decrease in household food insecurity and a 0.9-percentage-point (95% CI: −1.4, −0.5) differential decrease in child food insecurity. Households with low-middle income in USM-maintaining states experienced a 3.2-percentage-point (95% CI: −6.1, −0.3) differential decrease in household food insecurity but no differential change in child food insecurity. Households with lowest income in USM-maintaining states experienced no differential change in household food insecurity and a 3.8-percentage-point (95% CI: −6.2, −1.5) decrease in child food insecurity, although caution is required because the parallel trends assumption was violated.

Implementing statewide USM policies could contribute to decreased food insecurity among households with school-aged children.

## INTRODUCTION

Food insecurity, defined as limited or uncertain access to adequate food due to a lack of money or resources, increases children’s risk for impaired growth trajectories, poor diet quality, asthma, depressive symptoms, impaired social and emotional skills, worse academic performance, and lifelong consequences related to cardiometabolic health.1,2 One of the largest programs to address food insecurity for youth in the United States is the federal National School Lunch and Breakfast Program (NSLBP), which provides nutritionally balanced meals to approximately 30 million US children.3 Participation in NSLBP improves food security, academic performance, and nutritional outcomes for children.4–7

NSLBP operates by reimbursing schools for serving breakfasts and lunches that meet nutrition standards and other requirements.3 Importantly, these reimbursements are tiered based on the household income of each participating student, which also determines whether and how much students pay for their meals. Students with household incomes greater than 185% of the federal poverty level (FPL) pay full price, and schools are reimbursed the least for these meals; students with household incomes greater than 130% and less than or equal to 185% FPL pay a reduced price, and schools are reimbursed slightly more; and students with household incomes less than or equal to 130% FPL pay nothing, and schools are reimbursed the most for these students.

Underutilization of NSLBP limits its reach and impact, however.8 The paperwork that school staff and families must complete to maintain the tiered payment system is one driver of underutilization; children also report experiencing stigma in school cafeterias when receiving free or reduced-price meal benefits that discourages participation.9,10 Additionally, some children whose household income is low, but not low enough to receive free meals, thus qualifying them for reduced-price meals, still may not be able to afford to pay at all and thus forego the meals.10,11 Schools, groups of schools, or districts with high proportions of students eligible for free or reduced-price meals can opt to address these challenges by participating in the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP), a universal school meals (USM) policy that allows individual schools or districts to be reimbursed by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for serving free breakfasts and lunches to all students, regardless of household income.12 However, CEP does not reach schools or districts who decline to apply or who have lower proportions of students with low household incomes, despite the fact that even districts with higher incomes can still have many students in need.

In March 2020, as part of a suite of efforts to offset threats to households’ food access and economic stability due to the COVID-19 pandemic, Congress authorized the USDA to implement an emergency waiver that allowed for schools to serve meals to all students at no cost, regardless of household income, through the end of the 2021–2022 school year.13 When this emergency waiver expired on June 30, 2022,13 most states returned to the pre-pandemic 3-tiered payment system, with some individual schools or districts returning to CEP. However, several states chose to maintain or readopt their own statewide USM policies.14 Although prior investigations have found that CEP increases meal participation and school attendance and decreases suspension rates and child food insufficiency at a school or district level,15,16 it is unclear how statewide USM policies—which can reach many more children, particularly those living in schools or districts that do not qualify for CEP—may impact children, and there has been no research to evaluate the impact of these USM policies on diet quality and food insecurity specifically. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by assessing whether those living in states maintaining or readopting statewide USM policies after the COVID-19 pandemic had lower probability of household and child food insecurity compared with those living in states that discontinued statewide USM, particularly among children with lower household incomes who would not normally qualify for free meals.

## METHODS

### Study Design and Sample

This quasi-experiment used serial cross-sectional data from households with at least 1 school-aged child (aged 6–17 years) participating in the 2012 through 2021 or 2023 through 2024 waves of the Food Security Supplement (administered in December each year) of the Current Population Survey, a nationally representative annual survey from the US Census Bureau (Supplemental Figure 1).17

### Measures

#### Primary Exposure

The primary exposure was living in a state that maintained or readopted a statewide USM policy after the COVID-19 pandemic, measured by households’ state of residence. From March 2020 through June 2022, all households in all states had adopted the pandemic-related federal emergency waiver for USM.13 Households were considered exposed if they lived in states that then maintained or readopted statewide USM policy after 2022 (adopters in 2022–2023 school year: California, Maine, Massachusetts, Vermont, Nevada; adopters in 2023–2024 school year: Colorado, New Mexico, Minnesota, Michigan)14,18; all other states discontinued statewide USM after 2022 and were considered unexposed (Supplemental Figure 2). Seven states were excluded due to having passed legislation that expanded eligibility of free school meals that was (1) not sustained for the 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 school years (Nevada, Connecticut, Maryland), (2) not statewide (New York), or (3) not free for all students (Arizona, New Jersey, Ohio).14

#### Outcome

The primary outcome was household food insecurity, measured using the 18-item US Household Food Security Survey Module19 with a 30 day reference period. Child food insecurity, a more severe form of food insecurity, was our secondary outcome, measured using a subset of questions from the same survey.

Covariates included year, the head of household’s self-reported age (aged 15–34 years, 35–59 years, 60+ years), sex (male and female), highest level of education (≤high school, some college or 2-year degree, ≥4-year degree), ethnicity (Hispanic and non-Hispanic), and race (white, Black, American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian, or Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, Multiracial, according to fixed categories provided by the US Census Bureau).20 Race and ethnicity were included based on previously documented associations with NSLBP participation and food insecurity.1,8 Heads of households also reported household income (continuous), household size, number of children, receipt of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits in past month, receipt of charitable food in past month, and metropolitan status.17 The ratio of household income to FPL was determined based on household size, year, and state and categorized as lowest income (≤130% FPL), low-middle income (>130% to ≤200% FPL with 200% FPL as the upper limit due to evidence that those above the reduced-price threshold of 185% FPL being in need of subsidized meals), and highest income (>200% FPL).11

### Statistical Analysis

Survey-weighted sociodemographic characteristics were calculated for pre-exposure (2012–2021) and post-exposure (2023–2024), stratified by exposure status. Survey-weighted proportions of household and child food insecurity were calculated for pre- and post-exposure periods, both overall and stratified by exposure status and income level (Table 1) as well as year (Supplemental Figures 3 and 4). Linear probability models were fit using a difference-in-differences approach to estimate the average change in probability of household food insecurity from pre-exposure (2012–2021) to post-exposure (2023–2024), comparing households living in the USM-maintaining states (exposed) with households living in states that did not extend USM after 2021 (unexposed). Data from 2022 were omitted from the primary analysis due to potential confounding arising from the expiration of the expanded Child Tax Credit (CTC) in December 2021 as well as expiration of emergency SNAP allotments, which have been shown to influence food security21; importantly, these competing events may have differentially affected exposed and unexposed states.22,23 Analyses were stratified by household income levels given expected differences in how USM extension would affect households in different income categories, who would be subject to different fees for school meals without USM. The difference-in-differences model equation is shown in the Supplemental Text.

Models accounted for year and household-level covariates including age, sex, race, ethnicity, highest level of education, number of people in household, income (continuous), receipt of SNAP benefits in past month, receipt of charitable food in past month, and metropolitan status of residence to account for possible differences in the distribution of sociodemographic characteristics between exposure groups and to increase statistical precision. To examine whether trends in household and child food insecurity were parallel between exposed and unexposed states before 2022, an event-study model with a difference-in-differences analytic framework estimated the association between a state extending its USM policy after 2022 and the probability of food insecurity, using a series of yearly indicators and their interactions with a binary indicator for whether the household lived in a state that was exposed or not. We evaluated whether the coefficients for the exposure-X-year interaction terms were significantly different from zero for years before 2021, with 2021 as the reference year (Supplemental Figures 5 and 6).24

The models calculated effect estimates that predict the probability of household and child food insecurity. Effect estimates were multiplied by the weighted exposed sample to predict the number of households affected by the change in probability of food insecurity. Design-based variance estimators accounted for the complex survey design, including clustering of households within states. The analysis used a complete case approach, excluding households with missing information on outcome variables (household food insecurity, child food insecurity) or covariates (receipt of SNAP benefits in past month, receipt of charitable food in past month, metropolitan status of residence), all of which were less than 5% missing.

Sensitivity analyses assessed whether results were robust to the inclusion of 2022 data, with 3 scenarios: (1) excluding households living in states that did not readopt statewide USM until the 2023–2024 school year, (2) excluding households living in states that were late statewide USM adopters and had expiration of emergency SNAP allotments before 2023, and (3) excluding households living in states that were late statewide USM adopters, had expiration of emergency SNAP allotments before 2023, and were categorized as having low cost of living.22,23

All analyses were conducted in R version 4.4.0.25 Supplement survey weights and replicate weights accounted for nonresponse and complex sampling for nationally representative estimates. Two-sided alpha was set at 0.05. The institutional review board of a private university determined this to be not human subjects research.

## RESULTS

The analytic sample consisted of 75 122 households with children aged 6 to 17 years in pre-exposure (2012–2021) or post-exposure (2023–2024) survey waves (Table 1). Household sociodemographic characteristics were similar in pre- compared with post-exposure periods. Heads of households living in states that maintained or readopted statewide USM, compared with those in states that did not, were more likely to identify as Hispanic, have household incomes greater than or equal to $150 000, and live in a metropolitan area.

Household food insecurity increased for households with children in all states and across all income groups from pre-exposure (2012–2021) to post-exposure (2023–2024), except for those with low-middle incomes in USM-maintaining states. In states that maintained or readopted statewide USM, the weighted, unadjusted prevalence of household food insecurity changed from pre- to post-exposure from 19.2% to 25.1% for lowest income, 14.7% to 13.2% for low-middle income, and 3.1% to 4.5% for highest income; in USM-discontinuing states, corresponding changes were 19.7% to 24.9% for lowest income, 15.1% to 17.3% for low-middle income, and 3.1% to 5.2% for highest income. Meanwhile, in USM-discontinuing states, the prevalence of weighted, unadjusted child food insecurity changed from pre- to post-exposure from 10.8% to 15.4% for households with lowest incomes and from 8.3% to 8.7% for households with low-middle incomes; in statewide USM-maintaining states, the pattern differed between households with lowest and low-middle incomes (from 10.4% to 11.7% for lowest income and 7.5% to 6.6% for low-middle income households). Child food insecurity remained minimal for those with highest income in all states. Similar patterns were observed for the adjusted marginal predicted probability estimates of household and child food insecurity (Figures 1 and 2).

In difference-in-differences analyses, living in a USM-maintaining state was associated with a 3.2-percentage-point differential decrease in the probability of household food insecurity among households with low-middle income (95% CI: −6.1, −0.3) from pre- to post-exposure compared with those living in USM-discontinuing states. This translates to approximately 2900 fewer households with household food insecurity in USM-maintaining states than what would have been expected without statewide USM. Additionally, maintaining USM policy was associated with a 1.3-percentage-point differential decrease in household food insecurity (95% CI: −2.1, −0.5) among households with highest income. For households with the lowest incomes, there were no significant differences in changes from pre- to post-exposure in household food insecurity by USM status (Table 2).

Meanwhile, for households with the lowest incomes, living in a USM-maintaining state was associated with a 3.8-percentage-point differential decrease in the probability of child food insecurity (95% CI: −6.2, −1.5) from pre- to post-exposure compared with those living in USM-discontinuing states; additionally, it was associated with a 0.9-percentage-point differential decrease in child food insecurity (95% CI: −1.4, −0.5) among households with highest income. For households with low-middle income, there were no significant differences in child food insecurity over time by state USM status (Supplemental Table 1). Supplemental Tables 2 and 3 show crude model estimates.

Regardless of USM status, the adjusted models (Table 2; Supplemental Table 1) suggested some racial and ethnic differences in both household and child food insecurity risk that varied by household income level. Black households had significantly higher risk of both household and child food insecurity compared with white households, but only among the highest-income group; meanwhile, households identifying as American Indian/Alaskan Native, Asian, or Hawaiian/Pacific Islander had lower risk of household food insecurity than white households, but only in the low- and low-middle-income groups. Those identifying as non-Hispanic ethnicity, meanwhile, had higher risk of household and child food insecurity than Hispanic ethnicity households in the lowest-income group, but lower risk in the highest-income group.

Tests of differences in pre-trends in household food insecurity between households living in states that maintained or readopted statewide USM compared with USM-discontinuing states from 2012 to 2020 compared with 2021 found substantial violations in the parallel trends assumption for the lowest-income group in particular (2013, 2014, 2017, 2018, and 2019) with fewer for the other income groups (2020 for low-middle income and 2014, 2016, and 2017 for highest income) (Supplemental Figure 5). Similar patterns were observed for child food insecurity for each income level (Supplemental Figure 6).

### Sensitivity Analyses

In all sensitivity analyses, similar significant associations were found between living in the 5 USM-maintaining states from 2022 to 2025 and risk of child food insecurity as the main analysis, as well as significant associations for household food insecurity for households with lowest and highest incomes; however, associations between living in USM-maintaining states and household food insecurity were no longer significant for households with low-middle incomes (Supplemental Tables 4–9).

## DISCUSSION

In this difference-in-differences analysis using nationally representative data, living in a state that maintained or readopted a statewide USM policy after the expiration of the pandemic-related federal emergency USM waiver was associated with significantly decreased probability of household food insecurity for households with children whose income is low, but too high to receive free meals under NSLBP, averting household food insecurity for more than 2900 households. In addition, maintaining statewide USM policies was also associated with reduced household and child food insecurity for households with the highest incomes.

These results suggest that statewide USM policies may have protected households with children with incomes too high to allow participation in free school meals (and several other safety net programs) from a general trend toward higher food insecurity risk. The observed increases in food insecurity overall are likely attributable to the expiration of pandemic-related policies and waivers for administering various safety net programs (such as pandemic Electronic Benefits Transfer [EBT], expanded CTC, increased allotments of SNAP benefits)—which had often set income-eligibility requirements that allowed for households with low-middle income to participate during the pandemic—combined with inflation and a spike in food prices after the pandemic.26–28

Our results echo a prior study finding that statewide USM policies were associated with child food insufficiency, a more acute measure of food hardship used during the pandemic yet not robustly tested for its validity and reliability.15 There are several plausible mechanisms through which USM policies could alleviate both household and child food insecurity. Serving free school meals reduces food expenditures for households and also makes participation more appealing given the reductions in paperwork and stigma. Prior literature has found that USM policies, such as CEP, have been associated with increased school attendance and school meal participation and decreased household food expenditures.29–31

Schools in USM-discontinuing states can operate a universal free school meals program by opting into CEP at a school or district level. CEP is associated with better health outcomes32,33; however, CEP’s reach remains limited as it can be used only by high-poverty schools and districts that opt into it. Many schools and districts choose not to opt into CEP due to concerns about cost; only schools or districts with an identified student percentage from low-income households above 62.5% receive full reimbursement from the federal government, leaving districts (or states, in USM policy states) to make up the remainder of the meal cost to still offer the meals for free if less of the district or school is low-income.34 Due to these constraints, a statewide USM policy may be a more feasible and effective strategy.

This study is the first analysis to assess the association of state laws that extend USM policies on household and child food insecurity, using nationally representative data and a robust quasi-experimental design with validated measures. There are several limitations, however, and our results should be interpreted with caution. The analysis was conducted with the assumption that all children in the sampled households were attending schools that served NSLBP meals, which could lead to exposure misclassification (eg, a child attends a private school). There is also likely exposure misclassification among children living in USM-discontinuing states, given that districts within those states could still have implemented USM using CEP. Because data beyond 2024 are not available, it is also unknown whether the observed association between statewide USM policies and lower probability of household and child food insecurity will persist. Lastly, difference-in-differences analyses assume that the exposure (maintaining or readopting statewide USM policy) is random and that other policies are not being implemented or deimplemented during the same time period. This assumption was not appropriate for 2022, however, due to the expiration of several pandemic-era assistance programs impacting households differentially in USM-discontinuing vs USM-maintaining states during that year, including the expanded CTC,22 whose expiration may have had larger impacts in states with higher costs of living22,35 (which the USM-maintaining states disproportionately were), and pandemic-related emergency SNAP allotments, which expired at different times for USM-discontinuing and USM-maintaining states.23,36 Indeed, in sensitivity analyses that attempted to include the 2022 data (and excluded later readopting statewide USM states), similar associations were seen between maintaining statewide USM and household and child food insecurity for households with the lowest and highest incomes, but not for households with low-middle incomes (Supplemental Tables 4 and 5), regardless of whether we excluded additional states from the unexposed group (based on timing of expiration of emergency SNAP allotments and low cost of living) in an effort to make them more comparable to the exposure group (Supplemental Tables 6–9). It is unclear whether this may have been due to the remaining competing differential effects of the expanded CTC, whether this is a result of lower power from the exclusion of later readopting statewide USM states, or whether this is because no true association exists. Additionally, when testing the parallel trends assumption, we observed violations of parallel pre-trends, particularly for households with the lowest income with consistently negative pre-exposure event-study coefficients (Supplemental Figures 5 and 6). These violations make the results for households with the lowest income difficult to interpret and attribute to USM maintenance. For households with low-middle income, the 1 violation for household and child food insecurity was in 2020, which could be related to increased COVID-19–related school closures in December 202037 and data suggesting uneven implementation of meal programs (eg, grab-and-go meals, pandemic EBT) when schools are closed.38

## CONCLUSION

Children that are ineligible for free NSLBP meals under NSLBP’s existing 3-tiered payment system were protected from increasing trends in both household and child food insecurity from before 2022 to after if they lived in states that maintained statewide USM beyond 2022. As the number of states considering a statewide USM policy rises,39 this study suggests that implementing statewide USM could help alleviate food insecurity for thousands of children.
